items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A situation in which everyone has the same income, wealth or opportunities"?
items.answer: equality
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of equality.

items.stem: Explain the difference between equality and equity.
items.answer: Equality means equal shares; equity means fairness, which may involve unequal shares according to need or contribution. Equality can be measured; equity involves value judgements.
items.markingKey: Equality means equal shares; equity means fairness, which may involve unequal shares according to need or contribution. Equality can be measured; equity involves value judgements. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why equal outcomes may not be equitable.
items.answer: People differ in needs (e.g. disability, family size) and effort; giving everyone the same may be unfair to those with greater needs or who contribute more, so equity may require unequal treatment. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: People differ in needs (e.g. disability, family size) and effort; giving everyone the same may be unfair to those with greater needs or who contribute more, so equity may require unequal treatment. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In Country A the income shares of the five quintiles (poorest to richest) are 3%, 8%, 19%, 32%, 38%. Calculate the ratio of the richest 20% share to the poorest 20% share.

Read the source below.

Hypothetical income shares by quintile in Country Z: poorest 20% receive 5%, next 20% receive 10%, middle 20% 15%, next 20% 22%, richest 20% 48%.
— Hypothetical data

Using the data, calculate the ratio of the income share of the richest 20% to that of the poorest 20%, and explain what it suggests about equity.
items.answer: 48/5 = 9.6: the richest fifth receive almost ten times the income of the poorest fifth; whether this is inequitable is normative, but such a large gap suggests that the market distribution may be judged unfair.
items.markingKey: 48/5 = 9.6: the richest fifth receive almost ten times the income of the poorest fifth; whether this is inequitable is normative, but such a large gap suggests that the market distribution may be judged unfair. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Explain three reasons why market outcomes may be inequitable and discuss whether governments should aim for equality of outcome or equality of opportunity.
items.answer: Reasons: unequal ownership of factors/inheritance, differences in human capital and discrimination, market power and bargaining power, unequal access to education and health. Discussion: equality of opportunity preserves incentives but outcomes still unequal; equality of outcome may reduce incentives; most societies pursue both partly.
items.markingKey: Reasons: unequal ownership of factors/inheritance, differences in human capital and discrimination, market power and bargaining power, unequal access to education and health. Discussion: equality of opportunity preserves incentives but outcomes still unequal; equality of outcome may reduce incentives; most societies pursue both partly.

items.stem: Which of the following is a normative concept?
items.answer: Equity
items.markingKey: D. Whether a distribution is fair is a value judgement.

items.stem: Explain why inequality of opportunity can perpetuate income inequality across generations.
items.answer: Children from poorer families have less access to good education, health and networks, so they earn less as adults; their children face the same disadvantages – low intergenerational mobility.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Children from poorer families have less access to good education, health and networks, so they earn less as adults; their children face the same disadvantages – low intergenerational mobility. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why markets may fail to achieve equity.
items.answer: Markets distribute income according to ownership of factors and their market value; people with little wealth, low skills, disabilities or caring responsibilities earn little, and inheritance concentrates wealth, so outcomes may be judged unfair.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Markets distribute income according to ownership of factors and their market value; people with little wealth, low skills, disabilities or caring responsibilities earn little, and inheritance concentrates wealth, so outcomes may be judged unfair. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between wealth and income.
items.answer: Income is a flow of money received over a period (wages, rent, interest, profit); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time (property, shares, savings). Wealth is usually more unequally distributed than income.
items.markingKey: Income is a flow of money received over a period (wages, rent, interest, profit); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time (property, shares, savings). Wealth is usually more unequally distributed than income. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which inequality in Brazil shows the market's inability to achieve equity.
items.answer: Brazil's Gini coefficient was around 0.53 in 2022, among the highest in Latin America, despite falls since the early 2000s helped by the Bolsa Família cash-transfer programme. Unequal access to land, education and capital produces highly unequal market incomes; government transfers reduced but did not remove inequality.
items.markingKey: Context (Brazil's Gini coefficient was around 0.53 in 2022, among the highest in Latin America, despite falls since the early 2000s helped by the Bolsa Família cash-transfer programme.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Unequal access to land, education and capital produces highly unequal market incomes; government transfers reduced but did not remove inequality. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the market's inability to achieve equity.

items.stem: "A Gini coefficient of 0.25 shows more inequality than one of 0.45." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A lower Gini indicates a more equal distribution: 0.25 (e.g. Slovakia or Slovenia) is more equal than 0.45 (e.g. the US is around 0.39-0.41).
items.markingKey: A lower Gini indicates a more equal distribution: 0.25 (e.g. Slovakia or Slovenia) is more equal than 0.45 (e.g. the US is around 0.39-0.41). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Income inequality is necessary for economic efficiency."
items.answer: Some inequality provides incentives, but high inequality can harm efficiency and growth; the evidence suggests moderate inequality is compatible with strong performance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: income differences provide incentives to work, train and take risks; high rewards attract talent and entrepreneurship. Arguments against: high inequality can reduce growth (lower human capital investment among the poor, political instability); Nordic countries combine low inequality with high productivity; excessive inequality reduces social mobility. Supported judgement: Some inequality provides incentives, but high inequality can harm efficiency and growth; the evidence suggests moderate inequality is compatible with strong performance.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that market economies cannot achieve equity without government intervention.
items.answer: Some redistribution through government is needed for equity in practice, though growth, education and voluntary action also matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: markets reward ownership of factors, which is unequal; inheritance and discrimination persist; evidence: high pre-tax Gini coefficients in most countries. Arguments against: charities and community organisations redistribute voluntarily; economic growth can raise the incomes of the poor (absolute poverty falls); competition and education can increase mobility. Judgement: Some redistribution through government is needed for equity in practice, though growth, education and voluntary action also matter. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "marginal tax rate"?
options: Payments from the government to individuals for which no good or service is provided in return, such as unemployment benefits and pensions
A tax for which the average tax rate rises as income rises, so higher-income earners pay a larger proportion of their income
A curve showing the cumulative percentage of income received by cumulative percentages of the population, compared with a line of perfect equality
The tax rate paid on the last unit of income, ΔT/ΔY
items.answer: The tax rate paid on the last unit of income, ΔT/ΔY
items.markingKey: D. "marginal tax rate" is the tax rate paid on the last unit of income, ΔT/ΔY.

items.stem: A student claims that a flat-rate income tax of 20% is progressive because people with higher incomes pay more money. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Higher earners pay more money, but the same proportion of income, so a flat tax is proportional, not progressive.
items.markingKey: Higher earners pay more money, but the same proportion of income, so a flat tax is proportional, not progressive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a progressive tax and a regressive tax.
items.answer: A progressive tax takes a larger proportion of income from higher earners (rising average rate); a regressive tax takes a larger proportion from lower earners (falling average rate).
items.markingKey: A progressive tax takes a larger proportion of income from higher earners (rising average rate); a regressive tax takes a larger proportion from lower earners (falling average rate). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Finland's basic income experiment (2017-2018) shows transfer payments as a response to inequity.
items.answer: 2,000 unemployed people received €560 a month with no conditions; recipients reported higher well-being and slightly more days in work. An unconditional transfer reduced insecurity without the disincentives of means-testing, though the employment effect was small.
items.markingKey: Context (2,000 unemployed people received €560 a month with no conditions; recipients reported higher well-being and slightly more days in work.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: An unconditional transfer reduced insecurity without the disincentives of means-testing, though the employment effect was small. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transfer payments as a response to inequity.

items.stem: With reference to Brazil's Bolsa Família programme, explain how it illustrates conditional cash transfers to reduce inequity.
items.answer: Launched in 2003, it pays monthly cash transfers to low-income families conditional on children attending school and receiving vaccinations; it reaches over 20 million families. Transfers raise the incomes of the poorest immediately, while conditions build human capital and reduce future inequality.
items.markingKey: Context (Launched in 2003, it pays monthly cash transfers to low-income families conditional on children attending school and receiving vaccinations; it reaches over 20 million families.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Transfers raise the incomes of the poorest immediately, while conditions build human capital and reduce future inequality. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to conditional cash transfers to reduce inequity.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Governments should use direct provision of services rather than cash transfers to reduce inequity."
items.answer: Both are needed: services address long-run opportunity, cash addresses immediate poverty.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ensures spending on merit goods such as health and education; builds human capital and opportunity. Arguments against: cash gives people choice and dignity; transfers are quicker and cheaper to administer; evidence from cash-transfer programmes shows positive outcomes. Supported judgement: Both are needed: services address long-run opportunity, cash addresses immediate poverty.

items.stem: Which of the following policies aims to reduce inequality through direct provision?
options: A cut in the top income tax rate
items.answer: Free public education and healthcare
items.markingKey: B. Universal provision gives everyone access regardless of income.

items.stem: Hana writes: "Raising the minimum wage is the most targeted way to help the poorest households." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many of the poorest households have no one in work (pensioners, unemployed), so a minimum wage does not help them; transfers are better targeted.
items.markingKey: Many of the poorest households have no one in work (pensioners, unemployed), so a minimum wage does not help them; transfers are better targeted. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why means-tested benefits may create a disincentive to work.
items.answer: If benefits are withdrawn as income rises, a person taking a job or working more hours may gain little extra income (a high effective marginal tax rate – the poverty trap), reducing the incentive to work.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If benefits are withdrawn as income rises, a person taking a job or working more hours may gain little extra income (a high effective marginal tax rate – the poverty trap), reducing the incentive to work. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A country taxes income at 0% on the first $15,000, 25% on income from $15,000 to $40,000, and 45% on income above $40,000. Tomás earns $90,000. Calculate the tax paid, the average tax rate and the marginal tax rate, and state whether the system is progressive.
items.answer: Tax $28750; average rate 31.94%; marginal rate 45%; progressive
items.markingKey: Tax = 15,000×0% + 25,000×25% + 50,000×45% = 28750 [2]; average = 28750/90,000 = 31.94% [1]; marginal = 45% [1]; average rate rises with income ⇒ progressive.

items.stem: "A flat-rate income tax of 20% is progressive because people with higher incomes pay more money." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Higher earners pay more money, but the same proportion of income, so a flat tax is proportional, not progressive.
items.markingKey: Higher earners pay more money, but the same proportion of income, so a flat tax is proportional, not progressive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how a progressive income tax and transfer payments can reduce income inequality, using a Lorenz curve, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: line of equality and two Lorenz curves. The pre-tax (market income) curve lies further from the line of equality; after progressive taxes and transfers, the post-tax curve moves closer to the line, showing a lower Gini coefficient.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: line of equality and two Lorenz curves. The pre-tax (market income) curve lies further from the line of equality; after progressive taxes and transfers, the post-tax curve moves closer to the line, showing a lower Gini coefficient. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that governments should use direct provision of services rather than cash transfers to reduce inequity.
items.answer: Both are needed: services address long-run opportunity, cash addresses immediate poverty.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ensures spending on merit goods such as health and education; builds human capital and opportunity. Arguments against: cash gives people choice and dignity; transfers are quicker and cheaper to administer; evidence from cash-transfer programmes shows positive outcomes. Supported judgement: Both are needed: services address long-run opportunity, cash addresses immediate poverty. Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. items.stem: "Progressive income taxes are the most effective way to reduce income inequality." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Progressive taxes are important but work best combined with transfers, public services and policies that raise opportunity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: directly reduce the gap in post-tax incomes; raise revenue for transfers and services. Arguments against: disincentives to work and invest at high rates; tax avoidance and evasion, capital flight; do not help people with no taxable income – transfers and services needed; wealth inequality requires wealth/inheritance taxes. Supported judgement: Progressive taxes are important but work best combined with transfers, public services and policies that raise opportunity. Markbands (15 marks): IB Paper 1(b)/2(d) markbands [15]: Level 5 (13-15) relevant terms defined; theory explained clearly with an accurate, fully explained diagram where relevant; appropriate real-world examples; effective synthesis and a supported evaluation (short- vs long-run, stakeholders, assumptions, priorities). Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A piece of internal assessment of up to 800 words analysing a news article using economic theory, diagrams and one of the nine key concepts"?
items.answer: IA commentary
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of IA commentary.

items.stem: Distinguish between describing an article and applying economic theory to an article.
items.answer: Description repeats what the article says; application uses economic concepts, diagrams and terminology to explain why the events happened and their consequences.
items.markingKey: Description repeats what the article says; application uses economic concepts, diagrams and terminology to explain why the events happened and their consequences. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between evaluation and analysis.
items.answer: Analysis explains cause and effect using theory and diagrams (e.g. how a tax shifts supply); evaluation weighs the significance of these effects and reaches a supported judgement (e.g. whether the tax is the best policy).
items.markingKey: Analysis explains cause and effect using theory and diagrams (e.g. how a tax shifts supply); evaluation weighs the significance of these effects and reaches a supported judgement (e.g. whether the tax is the best policy). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Chloé writes: "All three IA commentaries can be on the same unit if they use different articles." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rubric requirements say each commentary must be based on a different unit of the syllabus (excluding Unit 1) and use a different key concept and source.
items.markingKey: Rubric requirements say each commentary must be based on a different unit of the syllabus (excluding Unit 1) and use a different key concept and source. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

'A city council in Bogotá has introduced a weekday charge for private cars that want to be exempt from the pico y placa driving restrictions. Officials say the revenue will fund public transport.'
— Example news extract for an IA commentary

Explain how a student could evaluate this policy in a commentary.
items.answer: Discuss effectiveness (PED for driving, availability of public transport), equity (wealthier drivers can pay to drive), use of revenue (public transport improves positive externalities), short- vs long-run effects, comparisons with London's congestion charge; reach a supported judgement.
items.markingKey: Discuss effectiveness (PED for driving, availability of public transport), equity (wealthier drivers can pay to drive), use of revenue (public transport improves positive externalities), short- vs long-run effects, comparisons with London's congestion charge; reach a supported judgement. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using an appropriate diagram, explain how a student could apply a negative externality diagram to an article about a new tax on single-use plastic bags.
items.answer: Diagram: market for plastic bags; MPB above MSB (negative consumption externality: litter, marine pollution); MPC = MSC. Market quantity Qm exceeds Q*; welfare loss shown. The tax raises the price paid, reducing quantity towards Q*; article data (e.g. bag use fell by 90% after England's 5p charge in 2015) can be referenced, and the key concept of sustainability applied.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: market for plastic bags; MPB above MSB (negative consumption externality: litter, marine pollution); MPC = MSC. Market quantity Qm exceeds Q*; welfare loss shown. The tax raises the price paid, reducing quantity towards Q*; article data (e.g. bag use fell by 90% after England's 5p charge in 2015) can be referenced, and the key concept of sustainability applied. IB Paper 1(a) markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) terms defined; clear, focused explanation; relevant, accurate and fully labelled diagram(s) that are explained. Level 3 (6-8) mostly accurate with some development. Level 2 (3-5) limited explanation or diagram errors. Level 1 (1-2) little understanding.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Using one key concept as a lens strengthens the analysis in an IA commentary.
items.answer: A well-chosen concept, used consistently in analysis and evaluation, strengthens the commentary; a superficially named concept does not.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: gives the commentary a clear focus; links micro events to broader economic ideas; rewarded explicitly in the criteria. Arguments against: forcing a concept can seem artificial; some articles relate to several concepts; the concept must be used throughout, not just named. Supported judgement: A well-chosen concept, used consistently in analysis and evaluation, strengthens the commentary; a superficially named concept does not.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that a commentary that uses a single well-explained diagram is better than one that uses several diagrams?
items.answer: Quality and relevance matter more than quantity: one or two fully explained, applied diagrams are usually best.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: limited word count makes full explanation of many diagrams difficult; depth of application is rewarded. Arguments against: some issues need two diagrams (e.g. a tax and its effect on a related market); criteria reward relevant, accurate diagrams, not a fixed number. Supported judgement: Quality and relevance matter more than quantity: one or two fully explained, applied diagrams are usually best. Markbands (10 marks): IB Paper 1(b)/2(d) markbands [15]: Level 5 (13-15) relevant terms defined; theory explained clearly with an accurate, fully explained diagram where relevant; appropriate real-world examples; effective synthesis and a supported evaluation (short- vs long-run, stakeholders, assumptions, priorities). Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Linking economic theory explicitly to the specific facts and data in the chosen article"?
items.answer: real-world application
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of real-world application.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "IA commentary"?
options: A tax for which the average tax rate falls as income rises, such as many indirect taxes as a share of income
A piece of internal assessment of up to 800 words analysing a news article using economic theory, diagrams and one of the nine key concepts
The tax rate paid on the last unit of income, ΔT/ΔY
Fairness or justice in the distribution of income, wealth and opportunities; a normative concept
items.answer: A piece of internal assessment of up to 800 words analysing a news article using economic theory, diagrams and one of the nine key concepts
items.markingKey: B. "IA commentary" is a piece of internal assessment of up to 800 words analysing a news article using economic theory, diagrams and one of the nine key concepts.

items.stem: Explain why students should choose articles that contain economic data and a clear issue.
items.answer: A clear problem or policy (e.g. a new tax) lets the student apply theory and diagrams directly, use the data to support analysis and evaluate the policy, meeting the criteria efficiently.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A clear problem or policy (e.g. a new tax) lets the student apply theory and diagrams directly, use the data to support analysis and evaluate the policy, meeting the criteria efficiently. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Rubric requirements say each commentary must be based on a different unit of the syllabus (excluding Unit 1) and use a different key concept and source.
items.markingKey: Rubric requirements say each commentary must be based on a different unit of the syllabus (excluding Unit 1) and use a different key concept and source. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using an article about Singapore's Certificate of Entitlement (COE) car quotas as an example, explain applying a key concept such as intervention in an IA commentary.
items.answer: Singapore limits the number of cars through COE auctions; COE prices exceeded S$100,000 in 2023. The quota can be analysed with a vertical supply curve for COEs, linking to negative externalities of congestion and evaluating equity effects.
items.markingKey: Context (Singapore limits the number of cars through COE auctions; COE prices exceeded S$100,000 in 2023.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The quota can be analysed with a vertical supply curve for COEs, linking to negative externalities of congestion and evaluating equity effects. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to applying a key concept such as intervention in an IA commentary.

items.stem: A student wants to write a microeconomics commentary on a news article about a city's new minimum wage. Identify two stakeholders and one evaluative point the student could discuss.
items.answer: Stakeholders: low-paid workers, employers (e.g. small restaurants), consumers, government; evaluative point: effect on employment depends on the elasticity of demand for labour; possible higher prices; short- vs long-run effects.
items.markingKey: Stakeholders: low-paid workers, employers (e.g. small restaurants), consumers, government; evaluative point: effect on employment depends on the elasticity of demand for labour; possible higher prices; short- vs long-run effects.

items.stem: "A good commentary summarises the article in detail before applying any theory." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A brief introduction to the issue is enough; marks come from applying theory, diagrams, terminology, the key concept and evaluation, not from summary.
items.markingKey: A brief introduction to the issue is enough; marks come from applying theory, diagrams, terminology, the key concept and evaluation, not from summary. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to an article about Indonesia's ban on palm oil exports in April 2022, explain how it illustrates selecting an article with a clear policy for a microeconomics commentary.
items.answer: Indonesia briefly banned exports of palm oil to lower domestic cooking-oil prices, causing world prices to rise. The article provides a clear intervention, effects on several stakeholders (domestic consumers, farmers, importing countries) and data, allowing diagrams, a key concept (intervention or interdependence) and evaluation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "equality"?
options: Making supported judgements, for example weighing short- and long-run effects, stakeholders, assumptions and priorities of a policy described in the article
Fairness or justice in the distribution of income, wealth and opportunities; a normative concept
A situation in which everyone has the same income, wealth or opportunities
A situation in which everyone has the same chances to succeed, regardless of background
items.answer: A situation in which everyone has the same income, wealth or opportunities
items.markingKey: C. "equality" is a situation in which everyone has the same income, wealth or opportunities.

items.stem: What is an example of a transfer payment?
items.answer: A state pension
items.markingKey: A state pension. Nothing is produced in return for the pension.

items.stem: Distinguish between applying economic theory to an article and describing an article.
items.answer: Description repeats what the article says; application uses economic concepts, diagrams and terminology to explain why the events happened and their consequences.

items.stem: Explain the difference between universal benefits and means-tested benefits.
items.answer: Universal benefits are paid to everyone in a group regardless of income (e.g. child benefit in some countries); means-tested benefits go only to those whose income or wealth is below a threshold, which targets help but can create disincentives.
items.markingKey: Universal benefits are paid to everyone in a group regardless of income (e.g. child benefit in some countries); means-tested benefits go only to those whose income or wealth is below a threshold, which targets help but can create disincentives. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why an IA commentary should focus on a small number of relevant diagrams.
items.answer: With only 800 words, one or two accurate, fully explained diagrams that are applied to the article's data show understanding better than many diagrams with little explanation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: With only 800 words, one or two accurate, fully explained diagrams that are applied to the article's data show understanding better than many diagrams with little explanation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ana writes: "Equity means everyone should receive the same income." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: That describes equality of outcome; equity is about fairness, which most people believe allows some differences in income.
items.markingKey: That describes equality of outcome; equity is about fairness, which most people believe allows some differences in income. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between universal benefits and means-tested benefits.
items.answer: Universal benefits are paid to everyone in a group regardless of income (e.g. child benefit in some countries); means-tested benefits go only to those whose income or wealth is below a threshold, which targets help but can create disincentives.
items.markingKey: Universal benefits are paid to everyone in a group regardless of income (e.g. child benefit in some countries); means-tested benefits go only to those whose income or wealth is below a threshold, which targets help but can create disincentives. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to an article about Singapore's Certificate of Entitlement (COE) car quotas, explain how it illustrates applying a key concept such as intervention in an IA commentary.
items.answer: Singapore limits the number of cars through COE auctions; COE prices exceeded S$100,000 in 2023. The quota can be analysed with a vertical supply curve for COEs, linking to negative externalities of congestion and evaluating equity effects.
items.markingKey: Context (Singapore limits the number of cars through COE auctions; COE prices exceeded S$100,000 in 2023.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The quota can be analysed with a vertical supply curve for COEs, linking to negative externalities of congestion and evaluating equity effects. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to applying a key concept such as intervention in an IA commentary.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how a Lorenz curve illustrates income inequality.
items.answer: Diagram: cumulative % of population on the horizontal axis, cumulative % of income on the vertical; 45° line of perfect equality; Lorenz curve below it. The further the curve sags from the line, the greater the inequality; Gini = A/(A + B), where A is the area between the line and the curve and B the area under the curve.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: cumulative % of population on the horizontal axis, cumulative % of income on the vertical; 45° line of perfect equality; Lorenz curve below it. The further the curve sags from the line, the greater the inequality; Gini = A/(A + B), where A is the area between the line and the curve and B the area under the curve. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how a progressive income tax and transfer payments can reduce income inequality, using a Lorenz curve.
items.answer: Diagram: line of equality and two Lorenz curves. The pre-tax (market income) curve lies further from the line of equality; after progressive taxes and transfers, the post-tax curve moves closer to the line, showing a lower Gini coefficient.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: line of equality and two Lorenz curves. The pre-tax (market income) curve lies further from the line of equality; after progressive taxes and transfers, the post-tax curve moves closer to the line, showing a lower Gini coefficient. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: A student claims that a good commentary summarises the article in detail before applying any theory. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A brief introduction to the issue is enough; marks come from applying theory, diagrams, terminology, the key concept and evaluation, not from summary.
items.markingKey: A brief introduction to the issue is enough; marks come from applying theory, diagrams, terminology, the key concept and evaluation, not from summary. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: That describes equality of outcome; equity is about fairness, which most people believe allows some differences in income.

items.stem: Explain why a universal basic income would be more costly than means-tested benefits, and one potential advantage.
items.answer: It is paid to everyone regardless of income, so total spending is much higher; advantage: no poverty trap or stigma, simple to administer, protects against job insecurity.
items.markingKey: It is paid to everyone regardless of income, so total spending is much higher; advantage: no poverty trap or stigma, simple to administer, protects against job insecurity.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Income inequality is necessary for economic efficiency.
items.answer: Some inequality provides incentives, but high inequality can harm efficiency and growth; the evidence suggests moderate inequality is compatible with strong performance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: income differences provide incentives to work, train and take risks; high rewards attract talent and entrepreneurship. Arguments against: high inequality can reduce growth (lower human capital investment among the poor, political instability); Nordic countries combine low inequality with high productivity; excessive inequality reduces social mobility. Supported judgement: Some inequality provides incentives, but high inequality can harm efficiency and growth; the evidence suggests moderate inequality is compatible with strong performance.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that progressive income taxes are the most effective way to reduce income inequality.
items.answer: Progressive taxes are important but work best combined with transfers, public services and policies that raise opportunity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: directly reduce the gap in post-tax incomes; raise revenue for transfers and services. Arguments against: disincentives to work and invest at high rates; tax avoidance and evasion, capital flight; do not help people with no taxable income – transfers and services needed; wealth inequality requires wealth/inheritance taxes. Judgement: Progressive taxes are important but work best combined with transfers, public services and policies that raise opportunity. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that using one key concept as a lens strengthens the analysis in an IA commentary.
items.answer: A well-chosen concept, used consistently in analysis and evaluation, strengthens the commentary; a superficially named concept does not.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: gives the commentary a clear focus; links micro events to broader economic ideas; rewarded explicitly in the criteria. Arguments against: forcing a concept can seem artificial; some articles relate to several concepts; the concept must be used throughout, not just named. Judgement: A well-chosen concept, used consistently in analysis and evaluation, strengthens the commentary; a superficially named concept does not. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: "Market economies cannot achieve equity without government intervention." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Some redistribution through government is needed for equity in practice, though growth, education and voluntary action also matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: markets reward ownership of factors, which is unequal; inheritance and discrimination persist; evidence: high pre-tax Gini coefficients in most countries. Arguments against: charities and community organisations redistribute voluntarily; economic growth can raise the incomes of the poor (absolute poverty falls); competition and education can increase mobility. Supported judgement: Some redistribution through government is needed for equity in practice, though growth, education and voluntary action also matter. items.stem: How many commentaries make up the IB Economics internal assessment portfolio?
items.answer: Three
items.markingKey: B. Each based on a different unit of the syllabus (not the introductory unit).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Lorenz curve".
items.answer: A curve showing the cumulative percentage of income received by cumulative percentages of the population, compared with a line of perfect equality
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a curve showing the cumulative percentage of income received by cumulative percentages of the population, compared with a line of perfect equality. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "average tax rate"?
options: Total tax paid divided by total income
A tax for which the average tax rate rises as income rises, so higher-income earners pay a larger proportion of their income
A situation in which everyone has the same chances to succeed, regardless of background
Making supported judgements, for example weighing short- and long-run effects, stakeholders, assumptions and priorities of a policy described in the article
items.answer: Total tax paid divided by total income
items.markingKey: A. "average tax rate" is total tax paid divided by total income.

items.stem: Distinguish between analysis and evaluation.
items.answer: Analysis explains cause and effect using theory and diagrams (e.g. how a tax shifts supply); evaluation weighs the significance of these effects and reaches a supported judgement (e.g. whether the tax is the best policy).
items.markingKey: Analysis explains cause and effect using theory and diagrams (e.g. how a tax shifts supply); evaluation weighs the significance of these effects and reaches a supported judgement (e.g. whether the tax is the best policy). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Ana writes: "A Gini coefficient of 0.25 shows more inequality than one of 0.45." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A lower Gini indicates a more equal distribution: 0.25 (e.g. Slovakia or Slovenia) is more equal than 0.45 (e.g. the US is around 0.39-0.41).
items.markingKey: A lower Gini indicates a more equal distribution: 0.25 (e.g. Slovakia or Slovenia) is more equal than 0.45 (e.g. the US is around 0.39-0.41). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.markingKey: Universal benefits are paid to everyone in a group regardless of income (e.g. child benefit in some countries); means-tested benefits go only to those whose income or wealth is below a threshold, which targets help but can create disincentives. items.stem: Explain the difference between applying economic theory to an article and describing an article.
items.answer: Description repeats what the article says; application uses economic concepts, diagrams and terminology to explain why the events happened and their consequences.
items.markingKey: Description repeats what the article says; application uses economic concepts, diagrams and terminology to explain why the events happened and their consequences. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between income and wealth.
items.answer: Income is a flow of money received over a period (wages, rent, interest, profit); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time (property, shares, savings). Wealth is usually more unequally distributed than income.
items.markingKey: Income is a flow of money received over a period (wages, rent, interest, profit); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time (property, shares, savings). Wealth is usually more unequally distributed than income. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that Raising the minimum wage is the most targeted way to help the poorest households. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many of the poorest households have no one in work (pensioners, unemployed), so a minimum wage does not help them; transfers are better targeted.
items.markingKey: Many of the poorest households have no one in work (pensioners, unemployed), so a minimum wage does not help them; transfers are better targeted. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a commentary that defines terms such as 'specific tax' and 'incidence' scores more highly on the terminology criterion than one that uses them without definition.
items.answer: The terminology criterion rewards relevant economic terms used appropriately throughout; defining key terms shows precise understanding and lets the reader follow the analysis.
items.markingKey: The terminology criterion rewards relevant economic terms used appropriately throughout; defining key terms shows precise understanding and lets the reader follow the analysis.

items.stem: In a country the richest 10% of households receive 40% of income and the poorest 40% receive 15%. Calculate the Palma ratio and explain what it indicates.
items.answer: Palma = 40/15 = 2.67: the richest tenth receive 2.67 times the income share of the poorest 40%, indicating substantial inequality.
items.markingKey: Palma = 40/15 = 2.67: the richest tenth receive 2.67 times the income share of the poorest 40%, indicating substantial inequality.

items.stem: A country taxes income at 5% on the first $12,000, 20% on income from $12,000 to $40,000, and 45% on income above $40,000. Isabel earns $45,000. Calculate the tax paid, the average tax rate and the marginal tax rate, and state whether the system is progressive.
items.answer: Tax $8450; average rate 18.78%; marginal rate 45%; progressive
items.markingKey: Tax = 12,000×5% + 28,000×20% + 5,000×45% = 8450 [2]; average = 8450/45,000 = 18.78% [1]; marginal = 45% [1]; average rate rises with income ⇒ progressive.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

'The government of Malaysia announced it would remove the blanket subsidy on diesel in Peninsular Malaysia from June 2024, raising the pump price by about 56%. Targeted cash aid will be given to eligible small businesses and farmers.'
— Example news extract for an IA commentary

Outline how a student could use this article for a commentary, naming a diagram and a key concept.
items.answer: Diagram: removal of a subsidy (supply shifts up from S − subsidy to S), price rises and quantity falls; key concept: intervention or equity; evaluate effects on consumers, firms, government budget and the environment, and the targeted aid.
items.markingKey: Diagram: removal of a subsidy (supply shifts up from S − subsidy to S), price rises and quantity falls; key concept: intervention or equity; evaluate effects on consumers, firms, government budget and the environment, and the targeted aid. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Briefly describe inequality in Brazil and explain what it reveals about the market's inability to achieve equity.
items.answer: Brazil's Gini coefficient was around 0.53 in 2022, among the highest in Latin America, despite falls since the early 2000s helped by the Bolsa Família cash-transfer programme. Unequal access to land, education and capital produces highly unequal market incomes; government transfers reduced but did not remove inequality.
items.markingKey: Context (Brazil's Gini coefficient was around 0.53 in 2022, among the highest in Latin America, despite falls since the early 2000s helped by the Bolsa Família cash-transfer programme.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Unequal access to land, education and capital produces highly unequal market incomes; government transfers reduced but did not remove inequality. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the market's inability to achieve equity.

items.stem: Briefly describe Finland's basic income experiment (2017-2018) and explain what it reveals about transfer payments as a response to inequity.
items.answer: 2,000 unemployed people received €560 a month with no conditions; recipients reported higher well-being and slightly more days in work. An unconditional transfer reduced insecurity without the disincentives of means-testing, though the employment effect was small.
items.markingKey: Context (2,000 unemployed people received €560 a month with no conditions; recipients reported higher well-being and slightly more days in work.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: An unconditional transfer reduced insecurity without the disincentives of means-testing, though the employment effect was small. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transfer payments as a response to inequity.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how a student could apply a negative externality diagram to an article about a new tax on single-use plastic bags.
items.answer: Diagram: market for plastic bags; MPB above MSB (negative consumption externality: litter, marine pollution); MPC = MSC. Market quantity Qm exceeds Q*; welfare loss shown. The tax raises the price paid, reducing quantity towards Q*; article data (e.g. bag use fell by 90% after England's 5p charge in 2015) can be referenced, and the key concept of sustainability applied.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: market for plastic bags; MPB above MSB (negative consumption externality: litter, marine pollution); MPC = MSC. Market quantity Qm exceeds Q*; welfare loss shown. The tax raises the price paid, reducing quantity towards Q*; article data (e.g. bag use fell by 90% after England's 5p charge in 2015) can be referenced, and the key concept of sustainability applied. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that governments should use direct provision of services rather than cash transfers to reduce inequity.
items.answer: Both are needed: services address long-run opportunity, cash addresses immediate poverty.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ensures spending on merit goods such as health and education; builds human capital and opportunity. Arguments against: cash gives people choice and dignity; transfers are quicker and cheaper to administer; evidence from cash-transfer programmes shows positive outcomes. Judgement: Both are needed: services address long-run opportunity, cash addresses immediate poverty. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples.
